question: What causes leg cramps together with numbness in the legs?
answer_short: Wallach ties severe leg cramps to calcium deficiency and the accompanying leg numbness to a B-vitamin deficiency.
answer_full:
Wallach pins the two symptoms on two separate shortfalls: the cramps on a calcium deficiency and the leg numbness on a vitamin B12 deficiency. He draws the reading from the Maybrick case, treating one man's cluster of complaints as a map of missing nutrients — cramps "so bad they were like iron bars" as calcium starvation, numbness as B12, and even the accompanying headaches as hypoglycemia or diabetes from chromium and vanadium deficiencies.

The calcium link fits his framework because calcium is what drives muscle contraction — he describes a muscle cramp as a "mini-convulsion" in the muscle. But he rarely blames calcium alone: cramps usually trace to a cluster of calcium, magnesium, potassium, selenium and/or vitamin E, with magnesium acting as the relaxer to calcium's stimulator, so a shortfall on either side can leave the muscle locked up. Because absorption matters as much as intake, his fix pairs liquid plant-derived colloidal calcium, magnesium and potassium with betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes to support digestion, at 75-200 mg three times a day before meals.
claim_text: In the Maybrick case Wallach reads leg cramps so severe "they were like iron bars" as a calcium deficiency, and the accompanying leg numbness as a B-vitamin deficiency — a vivid picture of mineral-starved legs.

question: Can a thyroid problem cause muscle cramps and aching legs?
answer_short: Wallach lists muscle aches, pains and cramps among hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's) symptoms.
answer_full:
Yes — muscle aches, pains, and cramps sit right on Wallach's list of hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's disease) symptoms, alongside fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, hair loss, brittle nails and depression. So a sluggish, underactive thyroid can genuinely be part of why the legs cramp and ache.

The reason traces back to how the gland runs. Wallach explains the thyroid concentrates the mineral iodine and combines it with the amino acid tyrosine to manufacture the hormone thyroxin, which sets your general metabolism, heart rate, body temperature and more. When iodine runs low the gland underperforms and hypothyroidism sets in — and he argues intake is usually low to begin with, made worse as people cut their salt on medical advice (copper is a required cofactor for using iodine, so copper-poor soils feed the problem too).

For the cramping and aching legs themselves, Wallach's treatment leans on the minerals muscles need to contract: liquid plant-derived colloidal calcium, magnesium and potassium, plus betaine HCl (a digestive acid) and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 mg three times a day before meals to help absorb them.
claim_text: Wallach lists muscle aches, pains, and cramps among the symptoms of hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's disease), so a sluggish thyroid can be part of why the legs cramp and ache.

question: What nutrients does Wallach say bone loss and ankylosing spondylitis need?
answer_short: Wallach says osteoporosis and ankylosing spondylitis (an inflammatory low-back arthritis) both trace to deficiencies of calcium, magnesium, boron, copper and sulfur.
answer_full:
Wallach gives both conditions the exact same nutritional fingerprint: calcium, magnesium, boron, copper and sulfur. In his Table 7-8 of degenerative diseases and their causes, osteoporosis and ankylosing spondylitis (an inflammatory, spine-fusing arthritis of the lower back) sit side by side with an identical list of missing minerals.

Calcium is the anchor. It's the most abundant mineral in the body — about 99% of it locked into the bones and teeth as hydroxyapatite — so when the diet runs short, Wallach says the body pulls calcium back out of the skeleton to keep blood levels up, thinning the bone until it fractures. The other four are the co-factors calcium needs to actually build and hold bone: magnesium, boron, copper and sulfur. He adds that the modern diet's excess phosphorus makes it worse by raising the body's calcium requirement.

He treats these as members of a much larger family — no fewer than 147 deficiency diseases he attributes to calcium shortage or imbalance, with both osteoporosis and ankylosing spondylitis on that list. The same table extends the pattern to bone spurs, heel spurs and calcium deposits, which he blames on calcium, magnesium and boron. For the arthritic, spinal-joint side, his joint-pain program pairs calcium and magnesium at 2,000 and 1,000 mg a day with copper at 2-5 mg, vitamin B6, cartilage and unsweetened gelatin, plus chiropractic for spine, rib and pelvic subluxations.
claim_text: Wallach attributes osteoporosis and ankylosing spondylitis, an inflammatory low-back arthritis, to deficiencies of calcium, magnesium, boron, copper and sulfur.
verbatim:
Table 7-8. Common Degenerative Diseases of Humans and Their Cause.
Osteoporosis: Ca, Mg, B, Cu, S
Arthritis (Ankylosing spondylitis): Ca, Mg, B, Cu, S
Hypertension: Ca, Mg, B
Bone spurs, heel spurs, Ca deposits: Ca, Mg, B

question: Can a chromium deficiency affect male fertility or sperm count?
answer_short: Wallach lists infertility and a decreased sperm count among the diseases of chromium deficiency — the same mineral he ties to blood sugar and diabetes.
answer_full:
Yes — Wallach lists infertility and a decreased sperm count as one of the diseases of chromium deficiency. It sits near the end of a long list (his Table 11-12) that is otherwise dominated by blood-sugar and mood disorders, and that's the key to how he sees it: chromium's main job in the body is glucose control — it's a core part of the glucose tolerance factor (GTF), the thing that makes insulin work. So the same shortage he blames for low blood sugar, type-2 diabetes and elevated cholesterol also, in his account, turns up as reproductive failure.

What makes it matter, in his telling, is how common and how self-inflicted the deficiency is. He cites the USDA's Richard Anderson that 90% of Americans are chromium-deficient, and he points the finger at dietary sugar directly: colas, fruit juices, honey, candy and table sugar flush chromium out through the urine, raising the natural rate of loss by 300% for a full 12 hours. He adds that the deficiency runs deeper when vanadium — the other trace mineral he pairs with chromium for blood-sugar control — is short at the same time.

question: What is Calcarea Fluor and is it used for varicose veins?
answer_short: The book's Schuessler cell-salt table points to Calcarea Fluor (calcium fluoride) for the 'relaxed' elastic fibers behind enlarged varicose veins and hemorrhoids.
answer_full:
Yes. Wallach's Rare Earths lists Calcarea Fluor — calcium fluoride, or "fluoride of lime" — specifically for enlarged varicose veins and hemorrhoids. In this account it's a component of the elastic fibers found in the surface of the bones, the enamel of the teeth, and the skin, muscle tissue and blood vessels. When it runs short, those tissues fall into what the book calls a "relaxed" condition — stretched-out and slack — which it treats as a predisposing cause of a number of diseases. So it's indicated wherever a problem traces back to slack elastic fibers: dilated blood vessels, hemorrhoids, enlarged varicose veins, hardened glands, and cracks in the skin.

That "relaxed elastic fiber" theme is one Wallach returns to on his own terms elsewhere, where he pins the same weak, stretched vessel walls on copper deficiency. Copper is the cofactor for lysyl oxidase, the enzyme that converts proelastin into elastin — the elastic fiber that gives veins and arteries their tensile strength — so when copper is low, elastin drops and the walls give way into spider veins, varicose veins, hemorrhoids and aneurysms. For preventing hemorrhoids and varicose veins he doesn't lean on any single ingredient: he recommends heavy supplementation with all 90 essential nutrients, eight to ten glasses of water a day, a high-fiber diet, and exercise.
claim_text: Rare Earths reprints Schuessler's cell-salt table, which lists Calcarea Fluor (calcium fluoride) — a component of the elastic fibers of skin and blood vessels — for the relaxed elastic fibers behind dilated vessels, hemorrhoids, and enlarged varicose veins.

of diseases. It is indicated in ailments which can be traced to a relaxed condition of elastic fibers, including dilation of the blood vessels,
haemorrhoids, enlarged varicose veins, hardened glands, cracks in the skin, etc.

question: Is there a cell salt or tissue salt for pimples?
answer_short: Wallach's cell-salt table names Calcarea Sulph (sulphate of lime) as the remedy for pimples and pustules of the face and other slow-healing skin eruptions.
answer_full:
Yes — Wallach names a remedy aimed squarely at facial pimples: Calcarea Sulph (Sulphate of Lime). He says it sits in the body's epithelial cells — the cells that make up skin and its linings — where it guards against cell breakdown and suppuration (the forming of pus). Run short of it and that pus-forming process drags on too long, so the eruptions that are slow to heal — his list runs from boils, carbuncles, ulcers and abscesses to the pimples and pustules of the face — are the ones that call for it.

That single remedy is only the surface, though. For facial skin eruptions Wallach leans hardest on nutrition: his acne rosacea program centers on essential fatty acids, zinc, vitamin A as beta-carotene, and digestive enzymes (betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes), on the view that a poor fat balance and weak digestion of the foods behind it are what drive the skin. And because the thread running through Calcarea Sulph is wounds that won't close, it belongs beside his topical (applied-to-the-skin) herbs for slow-healing wounds and ulcers — arnica, marigold (calendula), witch hazel and German chamomile among them.
claim_text: In Wallach's rundown of Schuessler's cell salts, Calcarea Sulph (sulphate of lime) is named as the remedy for slow-healing skin eruptions, including pimples and pustules of the face.

Calcarea Sulph (Sulphate of Lime) - is found in the epithelial cells in the blood. It acts as a preventitive of cell disintegration and
‘suppuration. A deficiency allows suppuration to continue too long; therefore, wounds that are too slow to heal (i.e.- catarrhs, boils,
carbuncles, ulcers, abscesses, pimples and pustules of the face) need this remedy.

question: Can a hair analysis reveal a hidden food allergy?
answer_short: When a hair test shows every mineral low, Wallach reads it as malabsorption -- frequently from an undetected wheat or cow's-milk allergy injuring the gut.
answer_full:
Yes — though the hair test flags the problem rather than naming the food. Wallach uses a hair analysis as a readout of your mineral status, and when every mineral comes back uniformly low, he reads it as a sign the minerals aren't getting into you at all. The two causes he names are maldigestion — hypochlorhydria, or low stomach acid, so food is never properly broken down — and malabsorption, a gut too damaged to take minerals up. That damage is classically celiac-type injury from a hidden wheat-gluten or cow's-milk (albumen) allergy, which leaves lesions in the lining of the small intestine.

Because even a good diet fails if you can't absorb it, Wallach doesn't stop at the hair test. To pin down the actual culprit food he pairs it with a pulse test on the things you eat often — the hair analysis reveals the malabsorption, and the pulse test hunts down the allergy behind it.
claim_text: Wallach says a hair analysis showing all minerals uniformly low points to malabsorption -- often from a hidden wheat gluten or cow's milk allergy damaging the gut.
verbatim: If all of the mineral levels in the hair analysis are universally low it indicates maldigestion ( hypochlorhydria - low stomach acid) and/or malabsorption ( celiac disease - wheat gluten or cows milk albumen allergy).

question: Are vegetarians and vegans at higher risk of weak bones?
answer_short: Wallach warns they can be -- because of high phytic-acid intake, vegetarians and vegans who don't supplement 'always' develop mineral deficiencies, including bone-building calcium and copper.
answer_full:
Yes — Wallach warns that vegetarians and vegans who don't supplement with minerals are set up for weak bones, and he pins it on phytic acid, a mineral-binding compound in the raw vegetables and grains these diets lean on. Phosphorus is the one mineral they rarely fall short of. But phytic acid latches onto other minerals in the gut and lowers their absorption, so in his telling these diets "always" leave the body deficient in the rest — calcium, copper, chromium, vanadium, lithium and zinc.

Calcium is the one that hits bone hardest: Wallach puts about 99% of the body's calcium in the bones and teeth, and he lists osteoporosis first among the diseases he attributes to calcium deficiency. He also frames osteoporosis not as an estrogen problem but as a mineral-and-absorption failure — which is exactly what a phytic-acid-heavy diet produces, unless the missing minerals are put back through supplementation.
claim_text: Wallach warns that vegetarians and vegans who don't supplement always develop mineral deficiencies -- including bone-building calcium and copper -- because of their high phytic-acid intake.

question: Do high-fat, high-meat diets cause high cholesterol?
answer_short: No — Wallach points to Eskimos eating ~90% meat and blubber with no cholesterol problems, thanks to fish EFAs that help the liver process cholesterol.
answer_full:
No — Wallach's go-to counter-example is the traditional Eskimo diet, which is roughly 90% meat and bone: whale meat and blubber, walrus, reindeer and fish. Despite eating almost nothing but animal fat, he says they have no cholesterol problems — and no heart disease or strokes either. So in his telling the meat isn't the culprit.

What protects them is the fish. The salmon and other cold-water fish in their diet are rich in essential fatty acids (the fats the body can't make and must get from food), and those EFAs are exactly what the liver needs to process cholesterol properly and to keep platelets from clumping together. Wallach credits EFAs with lowering blood cholesterol directly and with supplying the raw material for prostaglandins — compounds the body uses to help regulate blood clotting — which is why, in his account, a diet loaded with meat but also rich in fish fats doesn't translate into cholesterol problems, heart disease or strokes.

He treats dietary cholesterol itself as useful rather than dangerous, too: he calls the cholesterol in eggs and red meat critically important, since the myelin sheath that insulates the nerves is made almost entirely of cholesterol.

question: Can you actually see sugar affect a child's behavior?
answer_short: Wallach shows it with a child's drawings: a giraffe drawn before a sugary breakfast versus the messy version 90 minutes after — a simple visual test for sugar-driven ADD/ADHD.
answer_full:
Yes — Wallach shows it with the child's own hand. He puts two drawings side by side: a six-year-old's giraffe drawn before a high-sugar breakfast, and the same child's giraffe drawn an hour and a half later. The second is visibly degraded, and Wallach offers this as a simple at-home way to spot the ADD and ADHD he ties to a high-sugar diet low in chromium, vanadium and lithium (Cr, V and Li — trace minerals tied to behavior and blood-sugar control).

The reason the drawing falls apart on a timer, in his telling, is that sugar and refined flour flush chromium and vanadium out in the urine by as much as 300 percent, driving the low blood sugar whose symptoms include hyperactivity, irritability and being unable to think through simple problems. That's also why he treats ADD/ADHD by removing all sugar and alcohol from the diet and supplementing plant-derived colloidal lithium, chromium and vanadium — and he treats the drawing test as part of the therapy itself: teaching the child, and the whole family eating the same way, to see the connection between sugar and behavior.
claim_text: Wallach shows the effect of sugar on behavior with a child's own drawings — a six-year-old's giraffe drawn before a high-sugar breakfast versus the same child's degraded drawing an hour and a half after — as a simple at-home way to spot sugar-driven ADD/ADHD tied to low chromium, vanadium and lithium.

question: Do Epsom salts or magnesium help constipation?
answer_short: Wallach recounts that magnesium-rich Epsom water was famous as a very effective purgative for relieving constipation.
answer_full:
Yes — Wallach recounts that magnesium-rich Epsom water was prized as a very effective purgative and taken as an internal medicine for constipation. A purgative empties the bowel, so the water became famous for exactly that.

The story he tells begins in the summer of 1618, when a drought sent Henry Wicker of Epsom, a village south of London, hunting water for his cattle. They refused the small hole of bitter water he found — but that magnesium-rich spring soon proved valuable for both external and internal use. Lord Dudley North, under what Wallach calls a melancholy disposition (constipation and depression), drank the mineral waters as a medicine and found them a very effective purgative, and "Epsom Water" was rapidly accepted as an internal remedy and a purifier of the blood. In 1695 Nehemiah Grew finally isolated magnesium sulfate from the water, and by 1700 the town was drawing 2,000 visitors a day.

Wallach's own yardstick for the problem: if you are not having two to three bowel movements a day, he counts you constipated — and he says simple cases are very often solved by walking and eight glasses of water a day.

question: Can Pepto-Bismol or bismuth cause constipation?
answer_short: Wallach relays that bismuth, the active ingredient in Pepto-Bismol, reliably causes constipation.
answer_full:
Yes. Wallach relays a striking old observation that bismuth reliably produces constipation. He quotes the French physician Armand Trousseau (1801-1867), who noted that when a healthy person takes bismuth, constipation is the only effect worth noticing — it doesn't touch the nerves, the body's heat, the heartbeat, or the workings of the urine or sweat glands.

That side effect is really the flip side of what bismuth is used for. Wallach notes it's the active ingredient in the tasty pink Pepto-Bismol, sold over the counter to soothe an irritated gut and calm diarrhea and indigestion (dyspepsia). A medicine that quiets a runny gut naturally tends to slow it the other way too — hence the constipation. The compound has a long medical run: Adolf Kussmaul used bismuth to treat gastric ulcers back in 1868, and it's still on pharmacy shelves today.

question: Can prescription muscle relaxants make you dizzy?
answer_short: Yes - Wallach lists Flexeril, Norflex and Robaxin among muscle relaxants that cause dizziness, drowsiness and falls, and names calcium, magnesium, boron and lithium as the mineral replacement.
answer_full:
Yes — Wallach flags prescription muscle relaxants as a direct cause of it. In his drug-to-mineral tables he lists cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril), orphenadrine (Norflex, Norgesic) and methocarbamol (Robaxin) under "muscle relaxants and spasm relievers," noting they cause dizziness, drowsiness, fainting and falls.

Rather than the drug, he offers a "mineral replacement" — calcium, magnesium, boron and lithium — to address the underlying need with minerals instead. Boron earns its place here for a specific reason: he says it helps the body hold onto the very minerals it needs, cutting urinary calcium loss by about 40% and magnesium loss by a third within eight days. And the dizziness-and-falls pattern isn't unique to muscle relaxants — Wallach flags the same effects across the drugs he considers unsuitable for older patients, from tranquilizers and antidepressants to anti-nausea and arthritis medications, each paired with its own mineral replacement.
claim_text: Wallach flags common muscle relaxants - cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril), orphenadrine (Norflex), and methocarbamol (Robaxin) - as causing dizziness, drowsiness and falls, and offers calcium, magnesium, boron and lithium as the mineral replacement.
